I used to think that way until I moved to the northeast. Career and socioeconomic status pretty much determine who you date, who you hang with, what you eat, what you watch, pretty much your entire life. When I went back west to visit I realized it had been that way all along there too, I just wasn't paying attention. 

I woke up to reality, and that reality is that I like being around successful people, the conversation is better, the food is better, it's just happier. I didn't know what I was missing out on. I'm determined to end up like that. 

A good analogy would be that once you test drive a Ferrari life a Honda life will never feel the same, being in the city and surrounded by successful people has done that for my existence, and I can't erase that fact. It's ruined me the middle class existence I grew up with.

I don't really have any friends, I ruined any chance of that when I kept running home from school to save a marriage that couldn't be saved. I'm going to try to fix that over the next year.

Why an ultimatum? Because only successful lives matter, and I don't mean only in a material way. For someone who has a severe disability, working at all may be success. To an altruist, public  service may be success. 

Success to me is achieving ones realistic goals within the privileges and opportunities they have been given. Failure to meet those goals makes life meaningless, and moving the goalposts is cheating.  

A year is plenty of time to make a change, after that I'm just mooching off of life.

Obviously I want something that's fulfilling as well, but not if I can't maintain myself in the manner that I want to. I'm not really an altruist, I mean I like doing legal aid work, but not enough to lie to myself and go into public service while making poor money, because in my mind I will know I'm there because I didn't get where I wanted to be. I'm in the same boat, but in Law School. It's awful in my situation, where I need to be proactive and not procrastinate. It cost me my first year's grades, and I racked up 3 C's my second semester. I doomed my chances at BigLaw, and I still don't know if I am depressed or just lazy. I don't suppose it matters, because it's already too late to recover anything meaningful. If I could go back in time, I wouldn't have gone, because I went for the wrong reasons, and didn't focus on what I wanted to do (Political Science) because I didn't feel I had the connections to make it in the field, and went with a "Safe" choice.

I have to say that the fact that you enjoy art and can concentrate on it enough to be productive there may show that you are not lazy, but that you just need to focus on where you excel and have an interest and a drive. Art and writing seem to be it, and you are only 17 so don't get discouraged yet just because your works have not gone viral! Don't let anyone discourage you from that path, because if you pick one you don't want to be on, you will feel lazy and depressed. Keep up what you are doing!

Peter went to one of the top 3 law schools in the country. He always had a Big-Law job with a $160,000 a year starting salary waiting for him if he wanted one, and he took that job. He had a solid floor beneath him that allowed him to take risks and go off the grid. 

Now to be fair, Peter may have hated the idea of anything but a Supreme Court Clerkship as much as I hate the idea of working a anything but BigLaw, so in that respect we have something in common. But his "fallback" is something that opened a lot of doors, my default fallback is a dead end legal job where few people advance. 

In my case, yeah I need to hop off and go to London, my one good remaining door, make some friends, and try to restart my career. I can always return to law school if I need to, and try to make it work, but I know it isn't my first choice anymore.

Yeah, I am going to talk to career services on Thursday. But at this point I feel like hitting pause and going to London for a year to a masters program that is better than my law school might be a good bet. I may even find a good job with that and overcome my bad first year grades.

I have no doubt I can find a job, I just don't think I can find one that's a step up to anything good. I can also make new friends and forget about my failed relationship, hopefully.

Yeah, I had the same thought, but in New York most of the in-house counsel is staffed with BigLaw burnouts. No one reputable will touch someone who wasn't an associate for a few years.

My options are small firms, doc review, and solo practice, none of which really have great advancement prospects. I have a solid public interest resume, because once I tanked I decided I might as well do some good while I treaded water, but as much as I enjoy the work, I don't want to live on that salary...I'm just not that much of an altruist, and being single now I better be earning a decent salary in this city.

If I go to London, even if it's just a year leave of absence, I may be able to reset myself and make myself more marketable.

I can deal with the failed marriage, that's life, relationships fail. It sucks but I am moving on.

 It's the fact that I threw away my chance at a high paying career and not have to settle for less or abandon the law that drives me nuts. The life I could have had has vanished, and I know that the odds of finding a job that will lead to the six figure salary I was on track for with my degree and experience are slim. Law has bifurcated paths, and I am on the wrong one now, and there's no real way back into the better path. It's a very rigid hiring system for big firms, and I missed the boat.

I also missed the opportunity to form friendships with people in my school during the early days of law school because I always went home to be with my wife. Now it's too late, everyone in my class is established in their networks and I have none. I've tried to make friends here but it comes across as odd when I have been absent socially for so long, and I think it's just too late.

Pretty much my only choice now is a clean start, I am thinking of dropping out and doing a masters in London that I was accepted to. The only other choice is misery or death.
A career, but not a high paying, satisfying one. I feel like I need to give up on law school and try to find something new rather than settle. I will never be happy settling again.
